We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares discrete, continuous, and hybrid numeric encoding strategies for transformer-based models on EHR data, finding that hybrid token-based approaches with binning offer the best trade-off between precision and robustness, with bin count following a power-law scaling with dataset size.
AI.motivation: To determine how to best encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing for EHR data, given the trade-offs between numeric precision, optimization stability, and architectural flexibility.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, alongside real-world clinical prediction tasks.
AI.result: Approaches explicitly modeling value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks under suitable architectural constraints. Hybrid token-based approaches with binning prior to projection are more robust and broadly applicable, with optimal bin count following a power-law in dataset size. Models exhibit "good enough" rather than exact arithmetic computation; clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default for numeric encoding in EHR transformers.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a new class of failures in LLM agents called Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs), where agents get stuck in unbounded iterative execution. The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool that uses an Agent IR and Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to detect these failures. Evaluated on 6,549 repositories, it found 68 confirmed IAL failures across 47 projects with 91.9% precision.
AI.motivation: LLM agents executing iterative tasks via planning, tool use, and collaboration can get stuck in unbounded feedback loops when termination mechanisms are insufficient, leading to cost exhaustion, denial of service, context growth, and repeated side effects—a problem not addressed by existing tools.
AI.method: IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework-independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework-induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective bound.
AI.result: Evaluated on 6,549 LLM agent repositories: 74 potential findings reported, manual review confirmed 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.
AI.conclusion: IALs are a distinct and practical failure mode in LLM agents, and static analysis via IAL-Scan can effectively detect them with high precision.

title: A Cost-Aware, Paired Protocol for Auditing Dynamic Tool Synthesis in Agentic Video Question Answering
summary: Agentic Video Question Answering (VideoQA) systems invoke tools during inference, but their tool libraries are fixed, so recurring procedures are rebuilt from primitives on every question. Synthesizing composite tools could remove this overhead, but whether such expansion helps is hard to assess: final-answer accuracy, the standard metric, ignores inference effort, so it cannot reveal how a system shifts cost. We propose a cost-aware, paired protocol for auditing tool-augmented video agents. The protocol pairs two complete systems on the same input for each question and reports their net difference across accuracy and cost jointly. For each question, it sorts the paired outcome into one of six groups defined by joint correctness and by the change in visible tool calls, separating accuracy-preserving efficiency gains from harmful regressions. Significance is reported with McNemar's test and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We instantiate the protocol on Dynamic-SAGE, an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse on unseen questions, and evaluate it against the SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench. The audit reveals a multi-axis profile that a scalar accuracy comparison would miss: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p < 0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by roughly 28%, while shifting rather than reducing inference cost, as token usage rises 34% and cost 26%. Gains are largest on visual and open-ended questions and neutral on verbal and multimodal ones, and residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended questions where the pipeline does the most work. By measuring accuracy and cost jointly, the protocol shows where the pipeline-level difference is reliable and where it is not. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Dynamic-SAGE.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a cost-aware, paired auditing protocol for evaluating tool-augmented video agents, and instantiates it on Dynamic-SAGE, an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes reusable composite tools. Compared to the SAGE baseline, Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points while reducing reasoning turns and visible tool calls by ~28%, though token usage and cost increase. The protocol reveals multi-axis trade-offs that scalar accuracy alone would miss.
AI.motivation: Standard VideoQA evaluation uses final-answer accuracy, which ignores inference effort and cannot reveal cost-accuracy trade-offs. Existing agentic systems with fixed tool libraries rebuild recurring procedures from primitives on every question, creating overhead. A method is needed to jointly assess accuracy and cost when composite tools are synthesized.
AI.method: The authors propose a paired auditing protocol that: (1) runs two complete systems on the same input per question; (2) reports net differences in accuracy and cost jointly; (3) sorts paired outcomes into six groups based on joint correctness and change in visible tool calls; (4) uses McNemar's test and paired bootstrap confidence intervals for significance. They instantiate this on Dynamic-SAGE, which synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse, and evaluate against SAGE on SAGE-Bench.
AI.result: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p < 0.001), reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by ~28%, but increases token usage by 34% and cost by 26%. Gains are largest on visual and open-ended questions, neutral on verbal and multimodal ones. Residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended questions where the pipeline does the most work.
AI.conclusion: Joint accuracy-cost auditing reveals multi-axis profiles that scalar accuracy comparisons miss. The proposed protocol shows where pipeline-level differences are reliable and where they are not, providing a more complete evaluation of tool-augmented video agents.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus is a playground system (Janus-Core + Janus-Harness) for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management in AI agentic systems. It shows user input strengthens privacy/security, AI augmentation reduces cognitive load, and no single design works best across all contexts.
AI.motivation: The user's role in agentic permission management (where AI agents autonomously execute tool calls) remains underexplored despite many proposed approaches, raising pressing questions about what role users could and should play.
AI.method: Janus has two components: Janus-Core (modular agentic system supporting diverse permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (automated evaluation framework). Grounded in a conceptual model identifying key design axes for user involvement, six permission assistants spanning the design space were implemented and evaluated across three scenarios and three synthetic responders.
AI.result: User input is critical and significantly strengthens privacy/security; AI augmentation of user decisions helps reduce cognitive load; realistic user behavior like permission fatigue must be accounted for; no single design performs optimally across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: A more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems is needed. Janus is publicly available to support future research.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that integrates self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, atrophy classification, and reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art performance (88.17% accuracy for AD vs controls) and strong cross-cohort generalization for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and related dementias is challenging due to subtle and heterogeneous disease-related structural changes.
AI.method: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Evaluated on ADNI and OASIS cohorts with cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening.
AI.result: Achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. Largest gains in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. Demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization and systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

title: Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair
summary: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

AI.tldr: Refploit is an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework that improves Java vulnerability exploit reproduction from public references by analyzing failed agent trajectories, identifying completed subtasks and misleading directions, then applying focused recovery through differential execution and constraint derivation, achieving 80.2% reproduction rate on 143 vulnerabilities with 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories.
AI.motivation: Automatically reproducing runnable exploits from incomplete or unstructured public exploit references is challenging. Existing code agents often generate exploits that appear successful but fail to trigger actual vulnerable logic (e.g., replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions), making vulnerability assessment unreliable.
AI.method: Refploit first validates agent-generated exploits via differential execution. When ineffective, it analyzes reproduction progress, locates trajectory segments associated with that progress, derives constraints, and guides focused recovery to fix only the problematic parts while leveraging already completed subtasks.
AI.result: Evaluated on 172 exploit references for 143 Java vulnerabilities using DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit reproduces 138 exploits (80.2% rate), achieves 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories, and outperforms PoCGen and Codex with GPT-5.4. Adaptation to another code agent shows consistent improvements.
AI.conclusion: Failed agent trajectories contain useful information (completed subtasks and misleading directions) that can be leveraged for focused recovery. Refploit demonstrates that trajectory recovery is an effective and generalizable approach for automated vulnerability reproduction.

title: Anti-Prompt: Image Protection against Text-Guided Image-to-Video Generation
summary: Recent advances in Image-to-Video generation allow a single image to be animated into a convincing video under text guidance, raising serious copyright and privacy risks. We propose Anti-Prompt, an image protection approach that injects imperceptible perturbations into an image, inducing visible inconsistencies and structural failures in text-guided I2V generation. Our method is motivated by a simple empirical observation. When text guidance is removed from modern I2V models, generation quality degrades markedly, not only in motion realism but also in subject preservation, structural coherence, and temporal consistency. Building on this insight, Anti-Prompt exploits the model reliance on textual guidance by attenuating text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways. To further systematically evaluate protection effectiveness, we introduce a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol that provides interpretable, frame-grounded analyses of generation artifacts and inconsistencies. Experiments on two representative I2V architectures demonstrate that our method achieves strong protection performance while improving efficiency and cross-model transferability.

AI.tldr: Anti-Prompt protects images from unauthorized text-guided Image-to-Video generation by adding imperceptible perturbations that disrupt the model's reliance on textual guidance, causing visible inconsistencies and structural failures in generated videos.
AI.motivation: Recent I2V generation advances enable animating a single image with text guidance, raising serious copyright and privacy risks. Existing image protection methods are insufficient against text-guided I2V models.
AI.method: Anti-Prompt injects imperceptible perturbations that attenuate text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways, exploiting the observation that removing text guidance degrades I2V generation quality across multiple dimensions.
AI.result: Achieves strong protection performance with improved efficiency and cross-model transferability across two representative I2V architectures, validated by a new Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: Anti-Prompt effectively disrupts text-guided I2V generation by targeting the model's dependency on textual guidance, providing a practical defense against unauthorized video generation from copyrighted/private images.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT extends chain-of-thought reasoning into a semi-supervised learning framework by using unlabeled questions to generate pseudo reasoning chains, selecting reliable ones via answer-level semantic entropy, showing mixed results across math reasoning datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, and generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. The authors aim to leverage unlabeled data to provide pseudo reasoning supervision.
AI.method: Proposes Semi-CoT: sample multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimate answer-level semantic entropy, and select low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations for semi-supervised learning.
AI.result: Entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs (91.36%-100% precision). Small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K; negative transfer on AQuA; ceiling effect on MultiArith.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training strategies.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP extends the Gaunt Tensor Product using Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics to recover antisymmetric interactions missing in GTP, achieving CGTP-like expressivity with lower O(L^6) complexity for E(3)-equivariant networks in 3D atomistic modeling.
AI.motivation: The scalability of E(3)-equivariant networks is limited by the O(L^6) complexity of CGTP. The recently proposed GTP reduces complexity but lacks the ability to capture antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity.
AI.method: SpinGTP generalizes from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH), leveraging their algebraic properties to recover missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining GTP's asymptotic efficiency. It also provides a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for parity-odd components.
AI.result: Evaluated on Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 benchmarks. SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP, with superior performance on tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries due to explicit capture of antisymmetric paths.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous approach to achieving high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, overcoming the expressivity-efficiency trade-off of prior methods.

title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
summary: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

AI.tldr: KRCA is an end-to-end Root Cause Analysis system for hyper-scale microservice systems that uses a multi-stage pipeline combining API-level drilldown, skeleton-based causal graphs, and memory-augmented multi-agent reasoning to achieve superior accuracy (AC@1 0.88 for localization, 0.79 for classification) while reducing diagnosis time by 77.3% in production at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA methods struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of hyper-scale microservice systems, where failures are unavoidable due to numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment.
AI.method: A multi-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services, (2) skeleton-based causal graph instantiation from anomalous metrics as high-recall structural prior, (3) memory-augmented multi-agent framework for causality verification and failure report generation, combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning.
AI.result: AC@1 scores of 0.88 for root cause service localization and 0.79 for failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains; deployed in production for over six months reducing average diagnosis time by 77.3%.
AI.conclusion: KRCA effectively balances diagnostic accuracy with real-time production efficiency requirements, demonstrating strong performance and practical deployability for hyper-scale microservice systems.

title: Disentangling Pictorial Cue Understanding from Language Bias in VLMs via Depth Ordering Task
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, accepted to ECCV 2026 (30 pages, 13 figures, supplementary materials included)
summary: In this paper, we study depth perception of vision-language models (VLMs) to isolate the effects of pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision and language influences on model performance. To this end, we combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks: the VLMs are presented with images where one object is at different depth relative to other, otherwise identical, objects, and must determine whether the odd-one-out target is closer or farther to the observer. To create stimuli, we generate 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes while controlling the presence of individual pictorial depth cues, enabling a fine-grained analysis of cue-level contributions. Language effects are examined by varying referring expression clarity. We also introduce a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities. Applying this methodology, we create the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset with 37K real and synthetic images and 147K image-question pairs. Evaluation of 12 open-source and commercial models on O3-D shows under-utilization of depth cues and depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56%, with no model above chance level. At the same time, our metric reveals strong linguistic bias in the answers. Neither chain-of-thought (CoT) nor in-context learning (ICL) significantly improves performance, suggesting that static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. All code, the image generation pipeline, and the O3-D dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/lyiqian/o3-d.

AI.tldr: VLMs perform near chance (47-56%) on depth-ordering tasks from images, with strong linguistic bias overriding visual depth cues; neither CoT nor ICL helps, suggesting static images are insufficient for depth understanding.
AI.motivation: To isolate and disentangle vision vs. language influences on VLMs' depth perception by controlling pictorial depth cues and referring expression clarity, addressing the gap in fine-grained cue-level analysis of depth understanding.
AI.method: Combined depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks; generated 37K real/synthetic images (O3-D dataset) with controlled pictorial depth cues; varied referring expression clarity; introduced a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities; evaluated 12 open-source and commercial VLMs.
AI.result: All models scored 47-56% accuracy (none above chance); strong linguistic bias observed; CoT and ICL did not significantly improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs under-utilize pictorial depth cues and rely heavily on language priors; static images may be fundamentally insufficient for robust depth understanding in VLMs.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World is an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from interaction, using two cooperating agents (one acting, one synthesizing) with replay verification and Bayesian ontology error measurement. It achieves 20/25 game solves and 78.4 action-efficiency on ARC-AGI-3 without per-game training.
AI.motivation: Deep network world models are data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond training distribution, while program-synthesized world models (CEGIS) are data-efficient but have been limited to structured-state worlds with given object vocabularies and don't scale to pixel-rendered environments where object structure must be hypothesized flexibly.
AI.method: OPINE-World couples two cooperating LLM agents (actor and synthesizer) in a hypothesis-and-test loop. The synthesizer builds object-centric programmatic world models in code, verified via replay. Exploration is steered using ontology error, a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy. The framework operates without pre-specified object vocabularies, goals, or action semantics.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, OPINE-World solves 20 out of 25 games without per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against human baseline.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric programmatic world models can be learned online from pixel observations via cooperative LLM agents and inductive synthesis, achieving strong data efficiency and generalization without requiring pre-defined object vocabularies or per-game training.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that coding-agent RL execution infrastructure (containers, sandboxes, Kubernetes, VMs) has up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and a 1.8× spread in projected worker-hours for 1M trajectories, arguing that these substrates should be optimized as part of the training system, not just deployment plumbing.
AI.motivation: Current coding-agent RL treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail despite relying heavily on interactive software rollouts, missing opportunities for practical efficiency gains that compound at scale.
AI.method: Comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines, measuring cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: Up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and a 1.8× spread in projected worker-hours across substrates.
AI.conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, rather than treating them as mere deployment plumbing.

title: Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations
summary:
Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

AI.tldr: Archer is the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations, designed to detect semantic bugs in LLVM. Evaluated on 398 PRs, it discovered 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain bugs (e.g., miscompilations), revealing critical gaps in compiler code review capacity.
AI.motivation: Compilers are frequently updated but expert review capacity is limited, causing delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs. Automating code review with general agents faces challenges due to compiler complexity.
AI.method: Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends: (1) obligations guide analysis, and (2) a deterministic validation guard admits only findings backed by executable evidence. It targets LLVM compiler optimizations.
AI.result: On 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs: 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs were found buggy (introducing semantic bugs like miscompilations).
AI.conclusion: The findings expose a critical gap in review capacity for large compiler projects and demonstrate Archer's practical value as an additional reviewer.

title: Hidden-Shot: Towards One-Shot Task Generalization for Low-Level Vision Generalist Models
summary: Despite the intense engagement surrounding low-level vision generalist models, their effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks remains unverified. The primary challenge of developing an ideal generalist lies in achieving the ability to generalize from new unseen tasks, which also can be assessed by matched quantitative criteria. Existing methods have made some progress in prompt engineering but have not systematically explored this gap across a wide range of low-level visual tasks. Stimulated by the problem, we propose Hidden-Shot, an implicit prompt mechanism aimed at exploring low-level task adaptation in a vision generalist model. Specifically, the method extracts implicit visual task-based information, utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities in new tasks. The overall design performs direct injection in a cost-effective manner, while minimally altering the architecture of the original generalist model. Additionally, we introduce a data-driven evaluation framework termed C/U assessment to cover two basic scenarios, 3C4U (3 conventional and 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models and 3C7U (3 conventional and 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch, as a comprehensive assessment to systematically test the generalization ability of low-level generalist models. Experiments on seven and ten datasets outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model, respectively verified by 3C4U and 3C7U framework. Our presented Hidden-Shot approach demonstrates superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.

AI.tldr: Hidden-Shot proposes an implicit prompt mechanism for low-level vision generalist models that extracts implicit visual task information and uses global task-aware textural prompts to enhance one-shot generalization on unseen tasks. It also introduces a C/U evaluation framework (3C4U and 3C7U) to systematically test generalization, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing low-level vision generalist models have not verified their zero/few-shot generalization capabilities beyond learned tasks, nor have they been systematically evaluated with matched quantitative criteria. The gap between prompt engineering progress and comprehensive generalization assessment across diverse low-level visual tasks motivated this work.
AI.method: Hidden-Shot uses an implicit prompt mechanism that: (1) extracts implicit visual task-based information, (2) utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and (3) selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot adaptation. The design performs cost-effective direct injection with minimal architecture changes. A C/U assessment framework is introduced with 3C4U (3 conventional + 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining and 3C7U (3 conventional + 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch.
AI.result: Experiments on seven datasets (3C4U) and ten datasets (3C7U) outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model. Hidden-Shot achieves superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-Shot effectively bridges the generalization gap for low-level vision generalist models via implicit prompting and a structured evaluation framework, enabling strong one-shot task adaptation without sacrificing performance on learned tasks.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: This paper scales the SOLiD lie detection approach to larger models and more realistic preference-learning settings, finding favorable scaling where undetected deception drops from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at 99% true positive rate, and human labelers can be removed from fine-tuning without significant deception increase. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift, causing impractical false positive rates.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches like SOLiD that use lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers.
AI.method: Scales SOLiD to larger models (up to 405B parameters) and evaluates in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings.
AI.result: Undetected deception drops from 34% (1B models) to 14% (405B models) at 99% detector true positive rate. Expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from fine-tuning without statistically significant increase in deception.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD shows favorable scaling properties, but is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive false positive rates to impractical levels.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes conditional inference trees (CIT) and forests (CIF) as top-k feature-ranking methods, showing they control nodewise rejection with Bonferroni-corrected Monte Carlo permutation p-values, achieve competitive predictive performance (ranked 4th in classification, 3rd in regression), and identifies adaptive stopping and threshold search as major runtime factors (4.0-8.4× and 1.9-10.8× speedups respectively with minimal score changes), while highlighting that forest feature sampling can miss informative features in high-dimensional settings.
AI.motivation: To study CIT and CIF as top-k feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction, addressing the computational expense caused by repeated permutation tests and threshold searches, and to evaluate their performance and runtime characteristics.
AI.method: The authors analyze CIT and CIF using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. They study Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values for nodewise rejection control, and perform runtime ablations isolating adaptive stopping and threshold search effects.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. Turning off adaptive stopping increases fitting time by 4.0-8.4×, and using exact threshold search increases it by 1.9-10.8×, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Forest feature sampling can leave informative features out in sparse high-p simulations.
AI.conclusion: The results support CIF as a top-k feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks, with identified computational bottlenecks that can be optimized with minimal performance degradation.

title: Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS
summary: Open-source projects depend on a steady inflow of newcomers. A growing concern is that AI coding agents (tools such as Cursor and Claude Code that write code from natural-language instructions) will crowd them out, by absorbing the simple tasks that beginners start with and by making code harder to read. We give this concern a causal answer. Using GitHub code search we identify 1,888 projects that adopted an agent, signaled by their first commit of a configuration file. We apply difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to the 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. We find no evidence of crowding-out: across estimators newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after adoption (point estimates run from a small increase to, under the most conservative trend specification, a slight and insignificant dip), onboarding and retention are unchanged, and a sparse, correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels, which we cannot test for parallel trends) shows no decline. The feared mechanism is real but decoupled: adoption raises per-function code complexity (about +11% on a cognitive metric for Python, a quarter of the prior estimate, and +3 to 4% in cyclomatic terms across all languages), yet in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose (Python on the cognitive metric, and all languages on the cyclomatic metric), newcomer participation does not decline. These results suggest that, in established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out the human newcomers that a project depends on: the feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

AI.tldr: This study examines whether AI coding agents crowd out newcomers in open-source projects. Analyzing 1,888 projects that adopted AI agents using difference-in-differences analysis, the authors find no evidence of reduced newcomer inflow, onboarding, or retention post-adoption. While code complexity increases modestly (+11% cognitive metric for Python, +3-4% cyclomatic across languages), newcomer participation does not decline even in subsets where complexity rose. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.
AI.motivation: Open-source projects rely on a steady influx of newcomers, but there is growing concern that AI coding agents (e.g., Cursor, Claude Code) will crowd them out by absorbing simple beginner tasks and making code harder to read. This concern motivates a causal investigation into whether AI agent adoption negatively impacts newcomer participation.
AI.method: Using GitHub code search, the authors identified 1,888 projects that adopted an AI coding agent (signaled by first commit of a configuration file). They applied difference-in-differences analysis against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. They measured code complexity using cognitive and cyclomatic metrics across multiple programming languages.
AI.result: No evidence of crowding-out was found: newcomer inflow showed no significant decline after adoption (point estimates ranged from small increase to slight insignificant dip under the most conservative trend specification). Onboarding and retention were unchanged. A correlational measure (good-first-issue labels) showed no decline. Code complexity increased modestly (+11% cognitive metric for Python, +3-4% cyclomatic across languages), but newcomer participation did not decline even where complexity rose.
AI.conclusion: In established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out human newcomers. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

title: Boosting Infrared Small Target Detection via Logit-Domain Contrast and Adaptive Shape Refinement
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) remains challenging due to tiny target size, low signal-to-noise ratio, severe foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries in complex scenes. Existing methods usually rely on post-activation probability-domain supervision for discrimination, where weak targets and strong clutter may produce saturated and close probabilities, limiting weak-target discrimination. Meanwhile, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions mainly stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU), a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for IRSTD. Specifically, a Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) is introduced to enlarge the response gap between targets and informative hard negatives in the logit space, thereby enhancing weak-target discrimination. Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like overflow responses. In addition, False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples, further penalizing persistent high-confidence false alarms. Without introducing extra inference overhead, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the proposed method for infrared small target detection.

AI.tldr: AC-SLSIoU is a plug-and-play loss function for infrared small target detection that enhances weak-target discrimination via logit-domain margin constraints, refines contours via adaptive boundary suppression, and reduces false alarms via focal loss weighting, consistently improving detection accuracy and shape quality across detectors.
AI.motivation: Existing IRSTD methods using post-activation probability-domain supervision produce saturated and close probabilities for weak targets and strong clutter, limiting weak-target discrimination. Additionally, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU) with three components: (1) Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) enlarges the response gap between targets and hard negatives in logit space; (2) Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine contours and suppress halo artifacts; (3) False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples to penalize persistent false alarms.
AI.result: Without extra inference overhead, the method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability.
AI.conclusion: AC-SLSIoU is a plug-and-play loss function that addresses weak-target discrimination, boundary ambiguity, and false alarm issues in IRSTD, showing strong generalization across different backbone networks and detectors.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: A pipeline that uses a NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph and a heterogeneous GNN to rank candidate dataset pairings, then employs a three-agent LLM system to generate and evaluate structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, it produces 160 plausible hypotheses across multiple Earth-science domains.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on LLM-based hypothesis generation relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims, lacking grounding in structured, domain-specific knowledge. The authors aim to anchor hypothesis generation in a formal knowledge graph for Earth observation.
AI.method: (1) A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings from a NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph; (2) a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses.
AI.result: 160 hypotheses covering ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol-cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages. A 2×2×2 factorial experiment (GPT-5.2 vs. Claude Sonnet 4.6) shows stable rankings but judge-dependent absolute scores.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored dataset combinations. However, LLM-based evaluation of hypotheses suffers from judge identity effects, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and factual reliability of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, but hallucination risks increase at extreme ratios. Cross-domain performance degrades rapidly. The authors conclude that reliability assessment is essential for safe deployment in high-stakes domains like biomedicine.
AI.motivation: Prior studies on structured expert pruning primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect on factual reliability underexplored—especially in high-stakes domains like biomedicine where reliability is critical.
AI.method: The authors assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain (general domain) settings.
AI.result: Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, but hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. In cross-domain settings, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly.
AI.conclusion: Safe compression of MoE models depends heavily on task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without accompanying reliability assessment.

title: Understanding Software Defect Prediction: A Large-scale Empirical Study Across Uncertainty Quantification and Performance Evaluation
summary: Software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers produce probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear. We conducted a large-scale empirical study of probability-based UQ for SDP. We evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics for 16 representative classifiers. We analyzed these relationships under two prediction settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP), using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Results showed that UQ was highly context-dependent. Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; these correlations also varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable; classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating that uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects. Thus, UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives. Calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) for software defect prediction finds UQ is highly context-dependent; correlations between UQ and performance/calibration vary across prediction settings (within-project vs. cross-project), classifier types, and datasets, with many correlations weakening or reversing in cross-project scenarios.
AI.motivation: Software defect prediction classifiers produce probabilities for inspection prioritization and risk communication, but whether common uncertainty quantification metrics reliably indicate prediction performance and calibration is unclear, motivating a systematic empirical investigation.
AI.method: Evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics across 16 classifiers under two settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP) on 36 datasets and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) on 32 feature-compatible datasets.
AI.result: UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC and F1 under WPDP; correlations varied across classifier categories and datasets. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects.
AI.conclusion: UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives; calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics; transferred probabilities must be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

title: Mind the Gap: Standard 3DGS Evaluation Primarily Measures Near-Trajectory Interpolation
summary: Standard MipNeRF360-style 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) evaluation holds out every N-th frame -- but these frames have trained neighbors on both sides, so the metric measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than spatial generalization. We introduce a fair matched-count protocol that isolates this effect: both arms train on the same number of images and differ only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Our primary finding is a large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3~12dB -- several times the differences typically reported between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, is in two cases large enough to flip a method ranking under multi-seed confirmation, and -- crucially -- persists across three representation families, including a non-Gaussian volumetric neural radiance field (NeRF), so it reflects spatial coverage rather than any one representation. Diagnostically, it is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and tracks each view's angular distance to its nearest training view, a zero-cost signal that also guides capture planning; loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not, alone, be read as evidence of spatial generalization. Prior work notes protocol sensitivity; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to combine matched-count paired holdout, cross-representation quantification, and a diagnostic analysis Table 1. We describe a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits and baselines for 16 scenes, which we are preparing for public release.

AI.tldr: Standard 3DGS evaluation using interpolated holdout frames overestimates spatial generalization by 3-12 dB compared to extrapolation holdouts. This gap persists across representations, can flip method rankings, and is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component tied to angular distance to nearest training view.
AI.motivation: Current MipNeRF360-style evaluation protocols hold out every N-th frame, which measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than true spatial generalization, potentially misleading conclusions about method performance.
AI.method: Introduced a matched-count protocol where both arms train on the same number of images, differing only in holdout pattern: evenly spread (interpolation) vs. contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Tested across 3DGS, NeRF, and other representations with multi-seed confirmation.
AI.result: Found a consistent 3-12 dB gap between interpolation and extrapolation holdouts, large enough to flip method rankings in two cases. Gap persists across three representation families, dominated by diffuse/geometry-proxy components, and tracks angular distance to nearest training view.
AI.conclusion: Standard holdouts are useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not be read as evidence of spatial generalization. A spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits for 16 scenes is being released.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework that improves NPU kernel generation by incorporating hardware-aware knowledge through three modules (Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis, Bottleneck-Aware Retrieval, Effect-Driven Distillation), boosting accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieving up to 2.2x speedup over baselines.
AI.motivation: Developing high-performance NPU kernels is a critical bottleneck requiring manual navigation of implicit hardware constraints and memory hierarchies. LLMs fail on NPUs due to lack of hardware-specific priors, and naively transplanting code snippets causes runtime crashes and performance degradation despite compiling successfully.
AI.method: Hawk introduces three modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module using Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to couple error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module implementing 2D-Retrieval to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module leveraging LLM-driven semantic arbitration to prune errors and consolidate redundancies based on empirical execution feedback.
AI.result: Generation accuracy improved from 49.4% to 80.0%, with up to 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines on real-world NPU workloads.
AI.conclusion: Hawk effectively addresses the fundamental lack of hardware-aware priors in LLM-based NPU kernel generation through a training-free, knowledge-driven approach that synthesizes, retrieves, and distills hardware-specific knowledge.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: GRS-KAN integrates R-functions into KAN to encode geometric/logical constraints analytically, achieving up to 67% RMSE reduction on regression tasks with discontinuities while improving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Standard KANs lack explicit mechanisms to encode known geometric or logical constraints, making it difficult to handle discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries effectively.
AI.method: GRS-KAN combines KAN branches (learning smooth nonlinear structure) with differentiable R-functions (Rvachev's functions) that analytically encode geometric/logical constraints via R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions. Three variants are proposed: additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted.
AI.result: On regression benchmarks with circular/rectangular discontinuities, GRS-KAN reduces test RMSE by up to 67% compared to standard KANs, with improved boundary localization. The agnostic variant can automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric encoding via R-functions substantially improves predictive accuracy and interpretability in KAN-based regression, with the agnostic variant offering automatic prior selection capability.

title: Technical Debt Friction for Maintenance Prioritization: An Industrial Multi-Case Study
comment: Accepted for the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (Industry Track)
summary: Software-intensive organizations need effective ways to identify where maintenance and refactoring efforts will yield the greatest practical benefit. Although software analytics such as code health, hotspots, and coupling provide valuable signals, they do not always capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. This paper presents a multi-case industrial study of technical debt friction as a prioritization-oriented concept for identifying where technical debt most strongly affects maintenance and evolution. We investigate how practitioners interpret the concept, whether friction-related analysis aligns with perceived maintenance pain points and refactoring needs, and what broader maintenance and evolution insights friction can provide beyond individual refactoring candidates. To this end, we conducted structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases using analysis artifacts including code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. Our findings show that practitioners generally considered technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted together with complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction often aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention, although its practical relevance depended strongly on context. In addition, our exploratory project-level analysis suggests that friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns. These results indicate that technical debt friction is promising as a decision-support concept, but most effective when used with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-case industrial study of technical debt friction as a prioritization concept for identifying where technical debt most hinders maintenance and evolution. Through structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners using code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views, the authors found friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when combined with complementary views. File-level friction often aligned with known problematic areas and future maintenance attention, though context-dependent, and project-level friction distributions may reveal broader evolution patterns.
AI.motivation: Software-intensive organizations lack effective ways to identify where maintenance and refactoring efforts yield the greatest practical benefit. Existing software analytics (code health, hotspots, coupling) provide valuable signals but do not always capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice.
AI.method: Multi-case industrial study using structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases. Analysis artifacts included code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views.
AI.result: Practitioners found technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted alongside complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction aligned with known problematic areas and files receiving later maintenance attention, though practical relevance depended on context. Project-level analysis suggests friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns.
AI.conclusion: Technical debt friction is promising as a decision-support concept for prioritizing maintenance and refactoring, but is most effective when used with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence.

title: MVFusion-GS: Motion-Variance Guided Temporal Attention for High-Quality Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis for static scenes. Extending it to dynamic scenes via deformation fields has recently attracted significant attention, particularly for dynamic scene reconstructionband distractor-free. However, existing deformation networks lack explicit motion awareness: they neither capture long-term motion intensity nor exploit short-term temporal coherence, leading to inaccurate foreground deformation and pseudo-static residuals in the background. We present MVFusion-GS, a method that enhances deformation networks with two complementary motion-aware mechanisms. The Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics across time to estimate motion variance and uses it to guide dynamic-static separation during deformation prediction. The MotionFormer Temporal Attention module applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency. Extensive experiments on both dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, showing that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.
