AI.conclusion: Epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, though broader replication is needed before generalization.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
summary: Ultrasound image classification is essential for computer-aided diagnosis. However, current methods often neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and a lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption. To address these issues, we aim to develop a medical-prior module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines to enhance both diagnostic performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound classification that introduces domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, improving generalization while offering interpretable evidence. Specifically, a baseline branch follows conventional architectures and predicts image categories via a fully connected classifier. An attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors and produces human-interpretable decision cues. Finally, an adaptive decision module fuses the two branches in a data-dependent manner to yield the final prediction. Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks demonstrate that our approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhaobo253-crypto/AttrGuide.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound image classification that integrates domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to improve generalization and interpretability, while being lightweight and compatible with existing backbones.
AI.motivation: Current ultrasound classification methods neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption.
AI.method: The framework has three components: (1) a baseline branch using conventional architecture with a fully connected classifier for image category prediction; (2) an attribute-guided branch that injects domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to produce human-interpretable decision cues; (3) an adaptive decision module that fuses both branches in a data-dependent manner for final prediction.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks show the approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attribute-guided dual-branch framework effectively enhances both diagnostic performance and interpretability for ultrasound image classification by injecting clinical priors, and is easily integrable into existing pipelines.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an incremental expert bank for multi-source ECG deployment that freezes a pretrained backbone, assigns each domain an isolated classifier, uses a validation-calibrated margin rule for top-2 expert fusion when source metadata is unavailable, and identifies autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck.
AI.motivation: To enable multi-source ECG deployment where models must incorporate new data sources without retaining or replaying earlier raw ECGs, while addressing the practical challenge of selecting the correct expert when source metadata is unavailable at inference time.
AI.method: Uses frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features, adds balanced-softmax linear experts per domain, fits a lightweight MLP router on retained training features and domain labels, and applies a validation-calibrated margin rule to fuse the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection achieves 0.7915 Macro-F1 (close to offline independent-head reference at 0.7885). Without source IDs, MLP router reaches 0.7756 and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026) with 95% CI including zero. Top-2-to-oracle gap remains 0.0111-0.0133 across three domain orders.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous source inference is identified as the main remaining bottleneck; the method is not memory-free as frozen training features are retained for router updates.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) partitions memory into independent heads with a select-then-update strategy to prevent overwriting, significantly improving long-context retention (e.g., from <30% to 73.96% at 896K tokens) in a training-free manner.
AI.motivation: Recurrent memory agents suffer systematic performance degradation as context length grows because monolithic memory designs cause every update to risk overwriting previously retained content, with retention identified as the dominant bottleneck over memory capture.
AI.method: MHM partitions memory into independent heads with a stage-wise select-then-update strategy: at each step exactly one head is selected for update while remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting. MHM-LRU uses a Least-Recently-Updated heuristic for head selection with zero additional token overhead.
AI.result: Across 100K-1M token range, MHM-LRU substantially improves retention and end-to-end accuracy. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, retention improves from <30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization (specifically memory partitioning with overwrite protection) is a practical, training-free, and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory, shifting the retention burden from model behavior to architectural design.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing that curates 40 test-ready programs from open-source repositories, proposes characterization criteria, and demonstrates feasibility for scalability and fault-detection studies through controlled experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research lacks systematic benchmarks for empirical evaluation; studies rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, and available quantum programs are scattered without clear selection criteria, hindering fair comparison and reproducibility.
AI.method: The authors curate 40 programs from open-source repositories, apply systematic selection, refactoring, specification, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. They propose QST-oriented criteria (functionality, output behavior, development complexity, quantum-specific execution complexity) and conduct empirical studies with two recent QST approaches.
AI.result: Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties, supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks, and enables execution-cost and fault-detection studies. The experiments highlight backend-dependent effects that influence QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina provides a systematic, reproducible benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments, addressing the lack of test-ready, scalable quantum programs in the research community.

title: Plug-and-Play Volumetric Reconstruction for Compressive Sensing Light-Sheet Microscopy
summary: We investigate volumetric reconstruction for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), where fast volumetric imaging is achieved by encoding multiple axial planes into each camera exposure. To recover the underlying volume from highly multiplexed measurements, we propose a plug-and-play (PnP) framework that flexibly incorporates any user-specified denoiser into the reconstruction process. Building on a slice-based formulation, we further introduce an axial-coupled model that exploits correlations between adjacent slices to improve volumetric continuity. For efficient computation, we derive a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step in both the slice-based and axial-coupled formulations, and employ a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Under a weakly convex regularization assumption, we establish subsequential convergence of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed measurements, and provide practical insights into the comparative performance of commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a plug-and-play (PnP) reconstruction framework for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), incorporating a Woodbury-based data-consistency update and axial-coupled model to recover volumetric data from highly compressed measurements, with convergence guarantees under weak convexity.
AI.motivation: Fast volumetric imaging is achieved via CS-LSM but the underlying volume must be recovered from highly multiplexed (compressed) measurements; existing methods may not adequately handle the severe compression or ensure volumetric continuity.
AI.method: A PnP framework with slice-based and axial-coupled formulations; Woodbury-based update for data consistency; Gauss-Seidel sweep for denoising in the axial-coupled case; subsequential convergence analysis under weakly convex regularization.
AI.result: Successful recovery of cellular structures in synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data; practical comparisons of different denoisers within the PnP framework under CS-LSM.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PnP approach effectively reconstructs volumes from compressed CS-LSM measurements, with the axial-coupled model improving continuity, and the Woodbury-based strategy enabling efficient computation.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles is a learned module that edits gradients during finetuning to impart epistemic frames (e.g., "this is fictional") onto an LLM, achieving ~91% correct claim rejection vs ~9% via data annotation alone, while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: Standard data annotation (e.g., labeling text as fictional) fails to prevent language models from believing core claims in fictional documents (Negation Neglect), with models correctly identifying claims as fictional only ~9% of the time.
AI.method: Goggles is a module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient (not the data). During supervised finetuning, it edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives to impart a chosen epistemic frame. It is trained once per base model/frame/LoRA config, then applied frozen to unseen documents.
AI.result: Models trained with Goggles on unannotated documents flag content as fictional ~91% of the time (vs ~9% with annotation-only training), while GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline. The frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim.
AI.conclusion: Goggles provides a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing undesirable behaviors, and supports multiple epistemic frames (e.g., fiction, AI safety evaluation).

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: A two-stage learning pipeline combining an attention-augmented GRU wind estimator (0.40 m/s RMSE) with a PPO flight controller reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% over wind-blind baseline across 4-12 m/s winds, with the perception component contributing up to roughly half the benefit in strong winds.
AI.motivation: Small multirotor aircraft operating in the atmospheric boundary layer face turbulent winds comparable to airspeed that degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control.
AI.method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on simulated von Karman turbulence with power-law shear/veer estimates horizontal wind from onboard kinematics/dynamics; (2) frozen estimator's output feeds PPO flight controller; ablation decomposes improvement into kinematic vs. wind-perception components.
AI.result: Wind estimator achieves 0.40 m/s RMSE, 3.2° direction error, 0.861 skill score on vertical ascent. PPO controller reduces trajectory tracking error by 48% over PD baseline, winning 100% of episodes. Perception share grows from small in light winds to ~half of total benefit in strong winds. Controller degrades gracefully at 13-15 m/s where baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based wind estimation combined with RL control significantly improves multirotor trajectory tracking in turbulent winds, with the perception component becoming increasingly important at higher wind speeds due to quadratic drag scaling, and the system generalizes beyond training distribution.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight localized model editing framework that mitigates package hallucinations in LLMs by reformulating the problem as a package-validity boundary editing task. It uses risk-aware localization to identify relevant modules and boundary-aware LoRA adapters to reinforce valid packages while suppressing hallucinated ones. Results show significant reductions in hallucination rates across package recommendation (79.9% on edit prompts, 65.4% on unseen prompts), code generation (12.8%), and pip install recommendation (34.0%).
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from package hallucination—generating non-existent or invalid package names—which can be exploited in software supply chain attacks. Mitigating this is critical for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.
AI.method: BOUND formulates mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It first locates hallucination-related modules via risk-aware localization, then edits them with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality behavior.
AI.result: In package recommendation, Package-HR reduced by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts. It generalizes to other tasks: 12.8% reduction in code generation and 34.0% in pip install recommendation, while preserving valid package recommendations.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs, significantly reducing package hallucinations across multiple package-related tasks and improving the reliability of LLM-generated package-related outputs.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the prevailing DG approach of preserving visual expressiveness from large vision-language models, showing it propagates spurious cues. Instead, it proposes using the language embedding space as a primary information bottleneck for domain invariance, achieving SOTA results and shifting DG focus from representation improvement to invariance-enforcing supervision design.
AI.motivation: Domain Generalization (DG) aims to learn representations invariant to environment-specific variations, but existing approaches relying on large vision-language models inadvertently propagate spurious visual cues that tie representations to training environments, hindering invariant learning.
AI.method: The paper discards visual guidance and uses the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, treating it as a natural information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse backbones show state-of-the-art performance in domain generalization tasks.
AI.conclusion: The findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance, suggesting that language embeddings provide more robust guidance than visual features for domain-invariant learning.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW introduces agentic skill evolution for ComfyUI workflow construction, using typed graph editing, automated revert of invalid edits, region-level VLM verification, and a progressively disclosed skill library. It achieves best average scores across 4 benchmarks, 3 agents, and 2 backbones, with human preference over baselines.
AI.motivation: As agents handle repeated, domain-specific workflows, agent memory and reusable skills become critical for recalling workflow patterns, constraints, and user preferences from prior runs — a gap addressed in workflow-based image generation.
AI.method: Formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-organized tools, automatic reversion of invalid edits, a region-level VLM verifier for actionable repair suggestions, and a progressively disclosed skill library that distills trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Achieves best average image-generation evaluation scores across all six agent configurations (4 benchmarks × 3 agent models × 2 image backbones), outperforming verifier-only baselines, with human annotators preferring COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction tasks.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from equivariant world models' validity horizon, showing that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware using calibrated rollout-drift envelopes rather than on-manifold Lyapunov rates. The method controls certificate violations in frozen VN-JEPA models and reduces eventful-tail violations in a theorem-bed synthetic benchmark, though it does not universally dominate non-spectral schedulers.
AI.motivation: World models can certify how long their predictions remain valid, but there is no principled rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense based on that certification. The authors aim to turn the validity horizon into an operational sensing clock that works reliably in deployment.
AI.method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model, the authors derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals. They show that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware, using calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes instead of on-manifold Lyapunov rates. The method is evaluated on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model and a cue-conditioned theorem-bed synthetic benchmark.
AI.result: The clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards in VN-JEPA. In the synthetic benchmark, it remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations compared to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. In short-horizon regimes, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim of empirical dominance over all non-spectral schedulers. The method has limitations in short-horizon frozen model regimes and no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term was found.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion for testing code generated from prompts in LLM/agent-based programming, which measures how well a test suite satisfies prompt requirements via attention mechanisms and outperforms traditional code coverage by uncovering 30+% more faults.
AI.motivation: LLMs and autonomous agents are shifting software development from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals via prompts, which introduces new challenges for testing since prompts rather than code become primary artifacts; traditional coverage criteria are inadequate for this new paradigm.
AI.method: The authors propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a coverage criterion that operates at the prompt level using attention mechanisms of LLMs to measure how well a test suite satisfies prompt requirements. A simple instantiation based on attention boosting is evaluated across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA enhances Vision-Language-Action models for autonomous driving by adding driving-aware vision distillation and 2D trajectory-guided prompts, achieving state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs for autonomous driving rely on text-centric VQA and chain-of-thought data, which emphasize linguistic reasoning over action-grounded planning, resulting in representations that lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction.
AI.method: DriveTeach-VLA introduces two components: (1) Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder; (2) 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. The pipeline follows a three-stage process: DVD pretraining (what to see), TGP-guided SFT (where to look), and TGP-guided GRPO (how to act).
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The vision-guided learning pipeline explicitly teaches VLAs driving-relevant visual features and spatial reasoning, effectively bridging the gap between linguistic pretraining and action-oriented driving tasks.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Generic TB-Coverage is a coverage-aware MoE expert pruning method that uses generic text corpora (WikiText2, C4) to profile per-expert utility separately and enforce a fixed-budget coverage rule, outperforming random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base across multiple retention budgets and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE expert-pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score, which biases the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. This fails to account for cross-corpus expert utility diversity, and pruning without downstream calibration data remains challenging.
AI.method: Profiles per-expert utility separately on each generic corpus (WikiText2, C4), then enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask.
AI.result: On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets, the method improves average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks and reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4 compared to random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity. Gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning, improving performance without requiring downstream calibration data.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE is a framework that uses LLM-based evolutionary optimization to automatically discover preprocessing transformations for structured data, represented as Python programs. It improves time-series forecasting (3-19% error reduction) and tabular prediction (competitive accuracy with interpretability).
AI.motivation: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization, and the authors aim to leverage this for automatic feature engineering on structured data.
AI.method: EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, evolved using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback. Two instantiations: EFE-Time (invertible normalizations for time-series) and EFE-Tab (compact feature programs for tabular data).
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by 3%+ on average, up to 19% on COVID-Deaths dataset, improving recent TSFMs like Chronos-2. EFE-Tab matches or outperforms existing LLM-based feature engineering on tabular data, especially effective on decision trees.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data preprocessing.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: This paper studies file-level copying across the open-source ecosystem, finding 13 axial copy forms with distinct developer intents and risk profiles. Security vulnerabilities concentrate in vendored dependencies (88% of 17,314 CVE-risk commits), while license violations concentrate in direct source-code reuse (66% of 41,777 candidates). Both risks are invisible to standard dependency scanners.
AI.motivation: File-level copying is widespread but ungoverned software reuse that undermines supply-chain visibility by removing the four observable signals (provenance, maintenance, security, compliance) that package managers provide for declared dependencies. The scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse were previously uncharacterized.
AI.method: Mixed-method study using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, extracted 690,500 copy events and retained 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. Identified 13 axial copy forms and analyzed security and license risks across the full WoC graph.
AI.result: 13 axial copy forms exist with unreliable intent proxies. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old). Only 4.3% document origin; 2.0% are versioned. Security risk: 17,314 CVE-risk commits (88% in dependency-vendoring), 80% with CVSS >= 7.0, upstream-fix adoption 47%-84%. License risk: 41,777 candidates (66% source-code reuse), 39 verified high-star violations (kappa=0.752).
AI.conclusion: File-level copying creates significant visibility gaps in open-source supply chains that are form-specific. Both security and license risks reach packaged software and remain invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone, necessitating new detection and governance approaches.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: PanoGaussian reformulates 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos as synthesis with unseen regions, using panoramic trajectory guidance combined with a Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills panoramic features into explicit dynamic Gaussians to capture physical priors, achieving consistent synthesis under large viewpoint variations.
AI.motivation: Existing methods are limited to view interpolation and struggle to infer unseen regions beyond observed views. Camera-conditioned video generation lacks explicit 3D priors and suffers from inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations.
AI.method: PanoGaussian builds a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance, then proposes a Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture 4D scene physical priors.
AI.result: Achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations, overcoming the inconsistency issues of prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively due to scale/shape distortions from object motion; explicit dynamic Gaussian representation is needed to capture 4D physical priors.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, with tractable computation (O(K log K) instead of K! enumeration), convexity in offline setting, weak convexity in online setting, and strong empirical results in LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization for language model alignment focuses on pairwise supervision and robustness at the dataset/prompt/pair level, but neglects listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty caused by annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, or reward-model noise.
AI.method: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce (PL) objective that robustifies ranking labels conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss decomposes into nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, where the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order (O(K log K) vs K! enumeration).
AI.result: Offline: convex objective with O(ε^{-2}) sample complexity for global ε-suboptimality. Online: weak convexity with Õ(ε^{-2}) Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments show robust correction preserves clean-label performance and improves noise robustness in offline LLM alignment, and improves reward-model ranked candidate expansion and both reward-model/GPT-4 judge metrics in online alignment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust PL objective provides a tractable and theoretically grounded approach to handling ranking-label uncertainty in listwise preference optimization, with strong empirical benefits for LLM alignment under noisy supervision.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask that injects normalized graph topology into Transformer attention logits, enabling multi-hop propagation within a single layer via different adjacency matrix powers per head, achieving SOTA on 13 of 20 graph benchmarks without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers' all-to-all self-attention is ill-suited for graph data where interactions are sparse, structured, and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this with complex structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned constraints, introducing complexity and limited interpretability.
AI.method: X-LogSMask uses an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that applies a symmetrically normalized graph topology directly to attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. Each head uses a different power of the normalized adjacency matrix, giving it a defined structural radius for multi-hop propagation within a single layer.
AI.result: Across 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without modifying the Transformer architecture.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench is a benchmark evaluating how coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) handle underspecified DevOps instructions. Across 2,208 prompt variants, 55.8-67.8% of runs violate action boundaries, showing underspecification causes agents to guess rather than fail safely, with target ambiguity being especially problematic.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks overemphasize task completion and fail to assess safety under benign but underspecified instructions, leaving a gap in understanding how coding agents behave when operational boundaries are unclear.
AI.method: Built 69 task families from real incidents/CVEs across 4 DevOps domains and 9 control surfaces. Each task fixes environment and safe action while varying instructions along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. Uses deterministic side-effect-based oracles to classify outcomes (Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, clarification, refusal, deferment). Evaluated 2,208 prompt variants across 5 agent × model configurations.
AI.result: 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Underspecification does not cause failure but causes guessing. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality; blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity.
AI.conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy. Mitigations are needed at the model, harness, and system layers to address action-boundary violations in coding agents.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: TCA-Captioner is a framework that enhances temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning using an iterative refinement strategy (OCC) and a diagnostic benchmark (TCA-Bench), achieving state-of-the-art performance in generating temporally-coherent audiovisual narratives.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs for video understanding suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics in audiovisual video captioning.
AI.method: (1) Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework: an iterative refinement strategy for generating high-fidelity training data. (2) TCA-Captioner: optimized on curated high-density human interaction data to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. (3) TCA-Bench: a diagnostic benchmark with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning abilities.
AI.result: TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives, outperforming existing approaches as demonstrated by extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TCA-Captioner framework effectively addresses modality detachment and temporal incoherence in audiovisual video captioning by combining iterative data refinement, targeted model optimization, and a dedicated diagnostic benchmark for evaluating cross-modal alignment.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLM hidden state spaces, introducing the effective dimension d_ρ and kinematic features to characterize task difficulty and predict solution correctness from partial generation.
AI.motivation: While CoT reasoning has been extensively studied in terms of chain length and content, the internal geometry of reasoning trajectories in the hidden state space of transformers remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap by formalizing and analyzing the geometric structure of CoT trajectories.
AI.method: The authors formalize CoT reasoning chains as discrete curves in ℝ^d, characterizing them through spectral (eigenvalue spectra, effective dimension d_ρ), positional (mean position, dispersion), and kinematic (mean velocity, speed, speed dispersion) geometric functionals. Theoretical analysis links flatter eigenvalue spectra to harder tasks. Experiments use the MATH500 dataset for mathematical reasoning problems.
AI.result: The effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems on MATH500. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens, and these correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory provides a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality, with potential applications for early-stopping strategies in CoT generation.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: VLP is a human-in-the-loop framework that uses unambiguous NL-based documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and code, enabling users at all programming levels to validate and repair LLM-generated code via trace-link mismatch detection and formal verification.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code (via vibe coding) is unreliable due to intent-code mismatches. Existing validation methods are either fully automated (suffering from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility) or involve users only in partial artifacts (overlooking corner cases). A bug study reveals failures stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations, highlighting the need for detailed human feedback.
AI.method: VLP introduces (i) a literate language with unambiguous syntax and deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to focus user review, and (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation, verified via model checking.
AI.result: VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.
AI.conclusion: VLP effectively democratizes code validation for users of all programming levels by combining human feedback with formal verification through an NL-based literate documentation layer, significantly improving code reliability.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel Nested-UNet architecture for medical image segmentation that uses inner and outer attention units, squeeze-and-excitation modules for channel recalibration, and edge-aware loss to improve multi-scale context capture and upsampling, achieving superior generalization on three benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing segmentation methods struggle to capture information at multiple scales and perform effective upsampling across different datasets, leading to suboptimal generalization capabilities.
AI.method: A novel Nested-UNet architecture with (1) inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, (2) channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, and (3) an edge-aware loss function that emphasizes boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions.
AI.result: Tested on three publicly available benchmark datasets, the method demonstrates generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-enhanced Nested-UNet with channel recalibration and edge-aware loss improves segmentation generalization across multiple medical image datasets.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a case study on reformalization (autoformalization of formal proofs across systems), examining three translations of the Jordan Curve Theorem (Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, HOL Light→Agda) and analyzing design choices for practical reformalization pipelines.
AI.motivation: To study reformalization as a variant of autoformalization where the input is already a formal development (not natural language), and identify pipeline design choices that matter for translating proofs between different proof assistants.
AI.method: Three concrete reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. The paper analyzes these case studies to identify practical design choices for reformalization pipelines.
AI.result: Three successful reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem across different proof assistant systems, enabling analysis of pipeline design choices that impact practical reformalization tasks.
AI.conclusion: Reformalization is a viable approach for translating formal developments between proof assistants, with specific pipeline design choices (likely related to representation of logical foundations, proof structures, and tactic languages) being critical for practical success.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol to measure representational coupling between LLM agents. Through controlled experiments (~9,900 API calls), they find that text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803), image communication also homogenizes, group size moderates coupling direction (K=5 homogenizes, K=3 diversifies), cross-model replication shows extreme variation, and coupling is stateless (driven by prompt context, not cumulative updating).
AI.motivation: To determine whether inter-agent communication between LLMs causes outputs to converge (homogenize) or diverge (diversify), and to quantify this effect with a formal measurement protocol.
AI.method: Introduced BOUNDARY_SYNC protocol with Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline). Conducted controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) measuring coupling across text and image communication modalities, with various group sizes, cross-model replications, and ablation controls.
AI.result: (1) Text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803, d=1.30, p<0.001); (2) Image communication also homogenizes (CAF=0.834); (3) Group size moderates: K=5 homogenizes, K=3 diversifies (CAF>1.0); (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803); (5) Coupling is stateless and driven by prompt context.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

title: Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study
summary: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.
