AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively combines physical constraints with data-driven flexibility for wind power forecasting, generalizing across farms via zero-shot transfer.

title: RTE-FM-Dehazer: Radiative Transfer Equation Inspired Flow Matching for Real-World Image Dehazing
summary: Single-image dehazing aims to recover a clear scene from a hazy image and is generally formulated as an image-to-image translation task; however, it faces two limitations. Its performance depends heavily on the haze-formation priors embedded in the model. Prevailing methods adopt the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), whose assumptions of single scattering and homogeneous media are often violated, leading to residual haze and color drift. Moreover, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and existing synthesis approaches fail to reproduce the full complexity of natural haze. To address these issues, we present RTE-FM-Dehazer, a novel dehazing approach, together with a scalable data pipeline. Unlike the ASM, the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) jointly accounts for both scattering and absorption, naturally accommodating the non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media that characterize real hazy scenes. Motivated by the structural similarity between the RTE diffusion-absorption term and the ODE in flow matching, we introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, to steer the flow matching trajectory at each step. Next, leveraging modern vision-language models, we build an automated pipeline and release P-HAZE, a dataset of 50000 realistic hazy/clear pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates artifacts like residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RTE-FM-Dehazer uses a Radiative Transfer Equation regularizer and flow matching for single-image dehazing, paired with a 50K synthetic dataset (P-HAZE) generated via vision-language models, achieving state-of-the-art results on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image dehazing methods rely on the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), which assumes single scattering and homogeneous media—assumptions violated in real haze, causing residual haze and color drift. Also, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect.
AI.method: (1) Replaces ASM with the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to handle non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media. (2) Introduces a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, structurally similar to the ODE in flow matching. (3) Builds an automated data pipeline using vision-language models to generate P-HAZE, a 50K realistic hazy/clear dataset.
AI.result: Trained solely on P-HAZE, RTE-FM-Dehazer eliminates residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The RTE-based regularizer and realistic synthetic data pipeline effectively overcome the limitations of ASM-based dehazing, offering superior performance on real-world haze.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline to discover risks, compose executable safety cases, and adaptively test agents, revealing up to 93.9% attack success rates across four production agent frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed safety violations evaluated by hard-coded rules, which is costly to extend as agents evolve and cannot keep pace with emerging, complex safety risks from autonomous tool use.
AI.method: Vera instantiates software engineering testing principles through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration that continuously discovers and structures risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments; (2) combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases with concrete goals, programmatically constructed initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution where a control agent steers multi-turn interactions in isolated sandboxes and evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), Vera reveals substantial safety weaknesses with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. The released Vera-Bench contains 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM pre-training that uses first-moment-based statistics from AdamS to enable aggressive gradient sparsification (up to 99%) without quality loss, achieving up to 43.3% wall-clock reduction and 3.26× per-step speedup.
AI.motivation: Communication cost dominates LLM pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes. Existing methods like gradient sparsification (unstable for Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity) and quantization (bounded savings) are insufficient.
AI.method: SCAPE derives sparsification masks from AdamS's first-moment statistics (not raw gradients), partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, delays mask usage by one step to overlap synchronization with computation, and reconstructs second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer.
AI.result: On 32 GH200 GPUs: GPT-345M and Llama-500M preserve quality at 90-99% sparsity; Llama-500M achieves up to 43.3% wall-clock reduction; Llama-1.8B achieves up to 3.26× per-step speedup over dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that exploiting AdamS's first-moment stability enables aggressive communication compression via sparsification without compromising model quality, offering a practical and efficient solution for distributed LLM training.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is a novel tool for measuring complexity in LLM-integrated applications across both prompt and code layers, identifying 10 significant complexity metrics (7 new, 3 conventional) through empirical validation on 118 components, with prompt-layer metrics proving to be an independent dimension of complexity beyond code size.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics only operate at the code level, overlooking the behavioral logic embedded in the prompt layer of LLM-integrated applications, which blends natural language prompts with program code.
AI.method: HECATE uses Prompt-as-Specification (Hoare-logic-inspired formalism), identifies 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, generates 52 candidate metrics, evaluates them against 118 components from 18 open-source repos using version-history-based maintenance activity as proxy for complexity, and discards metrics losing significance after accounting for code size.
AI.result: Only 10 metrics survive: 7 new (measuring structural breadth like LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) and 3 conventional (RFC, Halstead N, V). Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate. Validation on 20 held-out components confirms generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity is an independent dimension of complexity in LLM-integrated applications, and structural breadth metrics outperform conventional volume-based metrics like Halstead N and V.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench is a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding that evaluates when to answer, not just what to answer, covering retrospective, present, future, and proactive settings across 22 datasets and 5,419 QA instances.
AI.motivation: Existing medical video benchmarks only assess answer correctness but ignore whether models answer at the right time, creating a gap between benchmark evaluation and real clinical deployment where AI must decide when to predict, defer, or alert.
AI.method: Integrates 22 medical datasets into 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive); restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows; supports single-turn and streaming evaluation; introduces proactive monitoring for alert timing; evaluates via responsiveness and post-evidence stability beyond answer correctness.
AI.result: Leading general-purpose and medical VLMs show a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings.
AI.conclusion: Current models struggle with time-aware reasoning in medical video understanding, especially in streaming and proactive scenarios, highlighting the need for temporally grounded AI systems for clinical deployment.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that integrates Memory-SAM for tongue segmentation, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured diagnosis, and RAG for clinical decision support, validated on a new large-scale dataset (MedTCM) and evaluated with a domain-specific metric (TDEU), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and reproducibility issues; existing multimodal AI approaches struggle due to the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, and the lack of large-scale standardized datasets.
AI.method: Three-stage architecture: (1) training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue diagnosis generation, (3) Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Validated on the newly introduced MedTCM dataset and evaluated using the proposed TDEU metric.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on the TDEU evaluation metric.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework addresses key challenges in AI-driven TCM diagnosis by effectively bridging visual and textual modalities, and introduces both a new dataset (MedTCM) and a domain-specific evaluation metric (TDEU) to advance the field.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP is a framework that recovers the training data composition (domain mixture weights) of a fine-tuned model directly from its weights, using model merging to simulate training trajectories and geometric features to predict domain proportions.
AI.motivation: Foundation model training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an access asymmetry where researchers study released models but cannot see their training distribution. Existing methods like membership inference only detect individual samples and cannot characterize global corpus composition.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned models via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory. From these simulated footprints in weight space, it extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP effectively recovers fine-tuned model training mixtures solely from released weights, offering a solution to the training data transparency problem without requiring access to the original training pipeline.

title: Search-based Testing of Vision Language Models for In-Car Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at the Industry Track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: In the automotive domain, in-car scene understanding (ISU) enables the detection of safety-critical events, such as driver distraction, and supports drivers or passengers by analyzing the in-car scene and adapting the environment (e.g., ambient lighting). The industry is increasingly exploring vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret camera-recorded in-car scenes and extract information for downstream reasoning tasks. However, VLMs may generate incomplete, erroneous, or misleading scene descriptions, highlighting the need for systematic testing. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, particularly in early design stages. In this paper, we present ISU-Test, an automated testing approach that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate ISU systems. By framing testing as an optimization problem and systematically modifying scene parameters, our method generates diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations. We evaluate ISU-Test on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two case studies: question answering and captioning, comparing against randomized scenario generation. Results show that ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage.

AI.tldr: ISU-Test is an automated testing approach for in-car scene understanding (ISU) systems that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing. It systematically modifies scene parameters to generate diverse in-car scenarios and detects failures in vision-language models (VLMs) on tasks like question answering and captioning. Evaluated on industrial and open-source VLMs, ISU-Test achieves up to 10x higher failure rates and 3.6x higher failure coverage compared to randomized baseline.
AI.motivation: In-car scene understanding (ISU) systems using vision-language models (VLMs) can generate incomplete or misleading descriptions, yet systematic testing is needed. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, especially in early design stages.
AI.method: ISU-Test combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing, framing testing as an optimization problem. It systematically modifies scene parameters to generate diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations.
AI.result: ISU-Test significantly outperforms randomized scenario generation, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across question answering and captioning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ISU-Test provides an effective, scalable, and automated approach for systematically testing VLMs in the automotive in-car scene understanding domain, addressing the limitations of costly real-world data collection.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a cross-crop 3D plant phenotyping framework powered by 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), replacing traditional COLMAP-based pipelines with feed-forward geometric recovery and 3D Gaussian Splatting. It achieves few-view, fast reconstruction from smartphone images, reducing reconstruction time from ~6.5 minutes to ~1.6 seconds while maintaining quality, demonstrating a streamlined route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D plant phenotyping is procedure-complicated and low-throughput due to multi-view imaging, fragile reconstruction pipelines, and costly geometry-to-phenotype extraction. Low-cost smartphone-based acquisition further suffers from limited view overlap and self-occlusion, amplifying these bottlenecks.
AI.method: The framework (1) replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, (2) uses geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, (3) enables few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement, and (4) converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. A cross-crop dataset with smartphone images and manual annotations was constructed.
AI.result: Across 26 plant sequences, 3D Foundation Models reduced average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy.
AI.conclusion: 3DFMs offer a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, enabling fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement from low-cost image acquisition.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions testing aviation-specific operational knowledge. Current best models (82.7% accuracy) fall well below expert-level reference (~95%), revealing a persistent gap that underscores the need for domain-specific evaluation before deploying LLMs in aviation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose benchmarks fail to measure whether LLMs reason safely about aviation-specific operational knowledge, yet LLMs are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations. The high-stakes, regulated nature of aviation makes this evaluation gap consequential.
AI.method: The authors created 300 multiple-choice questions from international standards (ICAO, US FAA regulations), airport ground operations material, and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by aviation practitioners. Models were evaluated using the Inspect evaluation framework, scored by accuracy under a standard multiple-choice protocol, with a rolling leaderboard.
AI.result: The strongest model (released 2026) reached 82.7% accuracy, improving gradually from ~75% in early 2025. This remains substantially below the informal expert reference of ~95% from aviation professionals.
AI.conclusion: A substantial and persistent gap below expert-level reliability remains. Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts framework with energy-based models, reveals that existing methods implicitly assume Gaussian residuals which mismatch real heavy-tailed behavior, and proposes a Cauchy expert-based approach that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which offer limited guidance for statistically scoring the usefulness of task-specific update directions across tasks during merging.
AI.method: Formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) framework, where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over merged parameters. Identifies that existing methods correspond to Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals. Observes heavy-tailed residual behavior and proposes a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts with a provably convergent inference procedure.
AI.result: Empirically demonstrates that directional residuals between merged and task-specific models are often heavy-tailed, exposing mismatch with Gaussian assumptions. The proposed Cauchy expert method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks and architectures.
AI.conclusion: Model merging can be better understood through a probabilistic inference lens; heavy-tailed expert designs (Cauchy) better capture real residual statistics and yield superior merging performance with a provably convergent inference procedure.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Coding agents face a human oversight bottleneck. Using traditional software engineering constraints (access control, network policies, coding conventions) transferred to agents is cheaper and more effective than agentic scaffolding. A controlled experiment showed backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% to 90.9% using constrained substrate plus a docs CLI tool.
AI.motivation: Human oversight is the bottleneck for coding agents; unconstrained agents create security risks, harm codebase scalability, and increase review cost.
AI.method: Transfer traditional human-team management methods (access control, network policies, coding conventions enforced by tooling) to coding agents. Conduct controlled experiment with a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspecting a Python codebase with 11 backdoors, comparing unconstrained vs. constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC docs CLI tool.
AI.result: Recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained) to 90.9% (constrained substrate + docs CLI). Substrate and tools contributed independently. Gains are largest in languages with fewer guarantees (Python) but principles extend to Rust.
AI.conclusion: Traditional software engineering constraints applied to coding agents are cheaper (in tokens) than recent agentic scaffolding and significantly improve oversight, especially in dynamically-typed languages.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for LDCT denoising that integrates anatomical-prior-guided conditioning, residual frequency-domain decoupling, and time-step-decoupling denoising to improve image fidelity, structural similarity, and anatomical detail preservation over existing methods.
AI.motivation: LDCT reduces radiation exposure but introduces quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation that obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Existing diffusion-based denoising methods suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model with three key components: (1) an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module that extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, (2) a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS) that enhances frequency-aware representations, and (3) a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3) that assigns representations to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 shows it retains task-relevant anatomical information.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT effectively addresses key limitations of existing diffusion-based LDCT denoising methods by incorporating progressive spectral and anatomical guidance, demonstrating superior performance in both image quality metrics and downstream task relevance for practical low-dose CT denoising.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: The paper connects fault tree analysis (used for predicting failures) with Halpern & Pearl's actual causality theory (used for explaining failures), showing how minimal cut sets can serve as actual causes, and classifying causality notions in terms of fault tree structure.
AI.motivation: Fault trees traditionally answer "what can go wrong?" via minimal cut set analysis, but lack a formal framework for answering "why has it gone wrong?" — a key question in failure diagnostics. The authors aim to bridge this gap by applying actual causality theory to fault trees.
AI.method: The authors apply Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality to fault trees, classifying different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and relating minimal cut sets to actual causes.
AI.result: A complete classification of different notions of actual causality in terms of fault tree graph and logical structure; demonstration that minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can be effectively used not only for predictive risk analysis but also for retrospective failure diagnostics by leveraging actual causality theory, with minimal cut sets serving as a bridge between the two perspectives.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, designed for beginning graduate students.
AI.motivation: To provide a structured, accessible introduction to diffusion models that bridges classical sampling methods and modern diffusion-based approaches, with rigorous proofs at multiple levels of depth.
AI.method: The material is layered into three tiers: (1) core definitions and identities proved in full, (2) representative estimates under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems presented with proof roadmaps.
AI.result: A pedagogical framework that traces a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers.
AI.conclusion: These notes aim to make diffusion models accessible to graduate students with a probability background but no prior exposure to SDEs, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

title: DL-VINS-Factory: A Modular Framework for Learned Visual Front-Ends in Visual-Inertial SLAM
summary: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) remains insufficiently characterized. We present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework that integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas--Kanade (LK) optical-flow tracking or LightGlue (LG) descriptor matching. All front-ends share a sliding-window Ceres back-end, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. We benchmark the system across the four datasets covering indoor, unstructured outdoor, aggressive-motion, and visually degraded conditions. Results show that learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM, but are not universally superior to classical tracking. Relative to the corresponding GFTT+LK baseline, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by $5\%$ in monocular odometry and by $7\%$ in stereo with loop-closure. On NTU-VIRAL, where aggressive aerial motion increases inter-frame viewpoint change, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by $12\%$. In Botanic Garden dataset, optical-flow tracking remains preferable, but learned keypoints still improve over the baseline GFTT, in which SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by $29\%$, while RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by $38\%$. On SubT-MRS, learned front-ends display varying degree of improvement based on individual cases. With TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin, all valid configurations run in real time between $29$--$47$ FPS in monocular mode and $18$--$33$ FPS in stereo mode for the EuRoC and NTU-VIRAL datasets. AnyLoc further confirms roughly $2$--$7\times$ more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. The implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/limshoonkit/DL-VINS-Factory-ROS2/.

AI.tldr: DL-VINS-Factory is a unified framework integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with optical-flow or descriptor-matching front-ends, a shared Ceres back-end, and optional DINOv2-VLAD loop closure. Benchmarked across diverse datasets, learned front-ends are viable but not universally superior to classical methods; they improve accuracy in specific scenarios (e.g., SuperPoint+LK reduces ATE by 29% on Botanic Garden, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by 5-7%) and run in real-time (29-47 FPS monocular, 18-33 FPS stereo) on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled VI-SLAM remains insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: The authors present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas-Kanade optical-flow tracking or LightGlue descriptor matching, a shared sliding-window Ceres back-end, optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization.
AI.result: ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by 5% (monocular odometry) and 7% (stereo with loop closure). On NTU-VIRAL, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by 12%. On Botanic Garden, SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by 29%, RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by 38%. On SubT-MRS, improvements vary per case. All valid configurations run in real-time at 29-47 FPS monocular and 18-33 FPS stereo on Jetson AGX Orin. AnyLoc finds 2-7× more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2.
AI.conclusion: Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM but are not universally superior to classical tracking; performance gains are scenario-dependent.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop method for domain-agent post-training that integrates data validation, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to manage adapter release risks. On five manufacturing batches, QLoRA-style SFT shows modest average gains but inconsistent batch improvements and high KL risks from GRPO. Application replay reveals RAG is essential for factual extraction, with a LoRA-SFT adapter improving value/evidence matching but increasing latency over base+RAG.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk, motivating a closed-loop pipeline that integrates data, training, evaluation, and release decisions rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. It combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide adapter suitability.
AI.result: On five anonymized manufacturing batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields average gains: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280, with reduced hallucination/wrong facts. However, only 3/5 batches improve; some regress. GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application replay shows RAG is necessary for factual extraction; a RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value/core fields/evidence matching over base+RAG but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying solely on training completion or a single offline score.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed neural networks by using additive weight initialization (shifting the mean, not scaling variance) for solving high-frequency PDEs. Two variants (FS-PIELM-L/G) achieve up to 5 orders of magnitude accuracy improvement over existing PIELM methods across 7 benchmark problems.
AI.motivation: High-frequency PDE solutions remain challenging for physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency components. Existing PIELM methods using scaling-based weight initialization amplify variance uncontrollably as target frequency increases.
AI.method: Instead of multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, FS-PIELM shifts the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity (additive initialization). Two variants: FS-PIELM-L (independent frequency magnitudes per neuron) and FS-PIELM-G (grouped neurons for robustness). It requires only a single linear solve.
AI.result: The linear variant (FS-PIELM-L) achieves best accuracy in 6 of 7 benchmark cases, with improvements of 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. Theoretical analysis shows frequency variance remains bounded near unity regardless of target frequency, unlike quadratic growth in conventional scaling methods.
AI.conclusion: FS-PIELM effectively overcomes spectral bias for high-frequency PDEs while preserving the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines. The additive initialization strategy avoids variance amplification, making it a principled and practical solution.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is an inference-time method that calibrates open-vocabulary object detection proposals by combining a localization-aware foreground score and a background-aware suppression score, improving novel object detection (e.g., +2.5 APr on OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14).
AI.motivation: VLM classification scores in open-vocabulary object detectors lack awareness of object position and scale, causing false positive novel activations on background proposals and poor ranking of true novel objects.
AI.method: ProCal computes a proposal prior via two scores: (1) localization-aware foreground score to capture whether a proposal contains an object region, and (2) background-aware suppression score to measure how much a proposal resembles background. These are combined to rerank proposals at inference time.
AI.result: ProCal improves APr by +2.5 on OV-LVIS using CLIPSelf ViT-L/14. It suppresses false novel activations on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial proposals.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-level localization-aware reranking effectively mitigates ranking miscalibration for novel objects, demonstrating that leveraging VLMs' inherent foreground/background classification ability can improve open-vocabulary detection without additional training.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STEER, a gradient-guided attack that translates refusal-inducing words into low-resource languages to bypass LLM safety mechanisms, achieving up to 93-96.7% attack success rates, and showing that English-only safety alignment fails to generalize across multilingual inputs.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs is predominantly conducted in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and code-switching, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently generate harmful responses for out-of-distribution inputs.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement) is a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most to refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent.
AI.result: Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and GCG. The prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% attack success rate without target model access.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs; improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a validation-time diagnostic, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF), to predict closed-loop performance of learned latent world models. CROF combines the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) with three structural regularizers. Applied to LunarLander v3 with an RSSM world model, CROF-selected checkpoints enable a model-based A2C policy to outperform a model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and also drive a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.motivation: Standard validation metrics like validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE fail to correlate with downstream closed-loop performance of world models, as they continue improving after closed-loop performance collapses. The paper seeks structural validation-time diagnostics from optimal-control theory to reliably predict closed-loop quality without online rollouts.
AI.method: Train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3 (shaped rewards). Evaluate 40 metrics against CEM-MPC return (oracle). Identify ROF as strongest single predictor. Combine ROF with three structural regularizers (likely related to observability, controllability, etc.) into CROF score for offline checkpoint selection. Use CROF-selected checkpoint for model-based A2C policy and zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.result: CROF-selected world model enables model-based A2C to outperform model-free A2C by ~24.5 return points with ~65x fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural validation-time diagnostics, particularly ROF and its composite CROF, offer reliable offline indicators of world model closed-loop performance, enabling efficient checkpoint selection and data-efficient model-based control.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic contact maps from text, improving physical plausibility by treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality with contact-guided sampling.
AI.motivation: Prior HOI generation methods suffer from physical artifacts (floating, interpenetration) due to poor contact modeling, relying on multi-stage pipelines that fail to capture temporally evolving contact.
AI.method: A single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates hand-object motion and distance-based contact maps. Contact is treated as an inner modality for joint training, with contact-guided sampling at inference to enforce consistency between contact maps and motion geometry.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods on GRAB and ARCTIC datasets.
AI.conclusion: Jointly generating contact as an auxiliary modality within a single-stage diffusion framework effectively addresses physical plausibility issues in text-driven HOI generation.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a frequency-aware Neural Architecture Search framework for Camouflaged Object Detection that automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, using a learnable wavelet transform in an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion guided by intuition rather than systematic search, which limits performance for detecting camouflaged objects with weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries.
AI.method: CamoNAS proposes a frequency-aware multi-resolution NAS framework that automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space. It also adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture with a learnable wavelet transform to complement the spatial stream.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of NAS for Camouflaged Object Detection is demonstrated, showing that automated architecture search outperforms traditional hand-designed COD models.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states using source-successor pairs, deriving transport tensors, circulation measures, and demonstrating affine covariance, estimator stability, and separation from infinitesimal geometry, with applications to analyzing recurrent neural network dynamics.
AI.motivation: Recurrent representations evolve as trajectories, but standard analysis measures representation geometry from static snapshots, missing directed temporal flow. The authors aim to capture finite-lag transport dynamics directly from observed state transitions.
AI.method: A conditional transport law Q_Δ is estimated via Gaussian source-smoothing, from which a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ (decomposing into conditional spread and coherent displacement) and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ are derived. Theoretical properties (affine covariance, stability, separation from infinitesimal Carre-du-Champ geometry) are proven, and a linear-Gaussian closed form is provided.
AI.result: Controlled experiments validate decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability. In repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in transport scale and coherent displacement trace; coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry captures recurrent dynamics missed by snapshot-based or infinitesimal measures, providing a principled framework for analyzing directed temporal structure in recurrent representations.

title: LLM-Empowered Multimodal Fusion Framework for Autonomous Driving: Semantic Enhancement and Channel-Adaptive Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by 2026 IEEE 37th International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications (PIMRC)
summary: Vision-radar fusion is central to robust autonomous driving, combining dense visual semantics with precise range and velocity measurements from radar. However, real-world fusion quality is fundamentally challenged by dynamically varying input quality, stemming from occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise. To address this, we re-frame the problem from static data fusion to channel-aware semantic reasoning and propose a Large Language Model-centric Semantic-layer Channel-aware Integrated Perception (LM-SCIP) framework. It places a Large Language Model (LLM) as a central reasoning core to fuse a local visual stream with a quality-varying external radar stream used to cover perception-blind spots. Concretely, LM-SCIP couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" to dynamically gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, in conjunction with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), then arbitrates between local visual cues and the channel-conditioned radar context. Finally, a decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Experiments on nuScenes and VIRAT validate our approach. On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, the model attains a 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results reveal that the proposed LM-SCIP enables a robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.

AI.tldr: LM-SCIP introduces an LLM-centric framework for vision-radar fusion that uses channel-aware semantic reasoning to dynamically adapt to varying input quality, achieving significant localization improvements on nuScenes (40% RMSE reduction) and VIRAT datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world vision-radar fusion suffers from dynamically varying input quality due to occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise, which static fusion approaches fail to address.
AI.method: Proposes LM-SCIP with: (1) hierarchical radar-vision encoder coupled with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) mapping link indicators to channel prompts; (2) LoRA-tuned LLM as central reasoning core with heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE) for arbitration; (3) decoupled multi-task decoder for localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction.
AI.result: On nuScenes: 40% localization RMSE reduction vs vision-only baseline under controlled radar toggle. On VIRAT: 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). Enables vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.
AI.conclusion: LM-SCIP demonstrates that reframing fusion as channel-aware semantic reasoning with an LLM core enables robust, quality-adaptive perception that gracefully degrades under poor radar conditions.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach is a self-evolving rubric framework that evaluates and enhances LLM agent skill-use along four process dimensions (selection, following, composition, reflection), providing better supervision than outcome-only metrics by distinguishing process quality from accidental task success.
AI.motivation: Final verifier success is too coarse for evaluating and training LLM agents on skill-use because agents may succeed via trial and error while using distractor skills, skipping steps, composing workflows incorrectly, or omitting final checks. Overlapping skills in realistic repositories make reliable skill-use difficult.
AI.method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. Rubrics evolve self-adaptively, and the external verifier is kept separate as an outcome signal to distinguish process quality from accidental success. Evolved rubrics serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Process-oriented rubrics that distinguish skill-use quality from outcome success offer a more effective framework for both evaluating and improving LLM agent behavior in realistic, overlapping skill repositories.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs.
